design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA-guided; no protocol or registration mentioned) of randomized trials of antipsychotics for amphetamine psychosis, a term the review uses to include methamphetamine psychosis. Eight databases plus ClinicalTrials.gov and grey literature were searched from inception to November 2018 with amphetamine keywords only. Six randomized trials with 314 participants were included: five head-to-head comparisons of two antipsychotics and one placebo-controlled trial of aripiprazole. Results are summarized narratively, trial by trial, and as standardized mean differences that the authors computed for each trial (Table 3); nothing is pooled. Risk of bias was rated with the Cochrane tool, trial quality with the Jadad (Oxford) score, and a GRADE level was given to each trial. Read: the full article on the publisher's site, including Tables 1 to 3 (rendered as text), author contributions, the conflict-of-interest statement, the editor and reviewer details and the reference list; Figure 1 (PRISMA flow diagram) is an image and was not read for values; the supplementary material (abstraction form, risk-of-bias tables) was not read.
can_establish: Which randomized trials of antipsychotics in amphetamine or methamphetamine psychosis had been published by November 2018, how they were designed, and what each reported on symptoms, side effects and retention, as this review summarizes them.
cannot_establish: Whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence and time achieve (five of the six trials had no placebo arm and the review's efficacy conclusion rests on improvement within each arm), whether any drug is better than another (nothing is pooled, the trials had 37 to 80 participants, and the per-trial effect sizes do not say which comparison or direction they express), or anything about treatment beyond 8 weeks or relapse after stopping (no trial followed participants after it ended).

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, EBSCOhost, ProQuest, the Cochrane Review Database, Medline Ovid and EMBASE, plus ClinicalTrials.gov and grey literature, from inception to November 2018 (Abstract › Methods; Methods › Search Strategy). 643 titles, 39 documents screened after title and abstract review, 8 full articles, 6 trials included (Results › Description of Studies). The trials were single-country hospital or outpatient samples from Thailand (2), Iran (2), China (1) and Malaysia (1), published 2005 to 2016 (Table 2). Arm counts are editors' sums from Table 2 and add up to the 314 of the abstract.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized controlled trials of an antipsychotic for amphetamine psychosis against another active drug or placebo, regardless of language, year or country, in adolescent or adult inpatients or outpatients (Methods › Eligibility Criteria; Types of Interventions). Excluded: cross-sectional, longitudinal, uncontrolled and non-randomized studies. Two full texts were excluded: a randomized trial that did not concern amphetamine psychosis (lithium and d-amphetamine in schizophrenia) and a non-randomized open-label study of aripiprazole (Results › Description of Studies; references 46 and 47). Every included trial excluded people with a DSM-IV history of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder (Results › Synthesis of Results).
sample.demographics: Participants aged 18 and over in five trials and 15 and over in one (Leelahanaj 2005); the review gives a mean age of 32 (SD 20.63) and states only that there were more men than women; five trials were in inpatient wards or a medical centre and one in outpatients (Results › Synthesis of Results; Table 2). Diagnoses: methamphetamine-induced or methamphetamine-associated psychosis in four trials (one also required a methamphetamine-positive urine test) and amphetamine-induced psychosis or amphetamine psychosis in two (Farnia 2014; Leelahanaj 2005) (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Trial-level completion and dropout are summarized in Table 3 and Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout, for example 93.1% completers on olanzapine against 65.5% on haloperidol in one trial and 33% discontinuation on aripiprazole against none on risperidone in another; one trial (Samiei 2016) reported no retention data.
sample.selection_effects: Only amphetamine keywords were searched (no methamphetamine term and no drug names), and a randomized trial of olanzapine against haloperidol in mental disorders induced by amphetamine-type stimulants, published in 2018 and cited in the discussion (Xue et al., reference 63), is neither included nor listed among the exclusions. The trials are small, short and mostly inpatient, so people with milder psychosis who are not admitted are not represented. The one placebo-controlled trial (Sulaiman 2013) was excluded by the 2021 network meta-analysis because its participants' psychotic symptoms had already subsided (study card sc_srisurapanont_2021); this review does not describe the participants' symptom level at entry.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study; the intervention is antipsychotic treatment. Psychosis was diagnosed by DSM-IV or DSM-IV-TR criteria in five trials and by clinical interview with a methamphetamine-positive urine test in one (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (the route is given only for Sulaiman 2013, oral, and not for the other five trials): quetiapine 100 to 300 mg/day against haloperidol 2 to 6 mg/day for 4 weeks (Verachai 2014); aripiprazole 5 to 15 mg/day against risperidone 2 to 6 mg/day for 25 days (Wang 2016); aripiprazole 15 mg/day against risperidone 4 mg/day for 6 weeks (Farnia 2014); aripiprazole 5 to 10 mg/day against placebo for 8 weeks (Sulaiman 2013); haloperidol 5 to 20 mg/day against risperidone 2 to 8 mg/day for 1 month (Samiei 2016); olanzapine 5 to 20 mg/day against haloperidol 5 to 20 mg/day for 4 weeks (Leelahanaj 2005) (Table 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported by the review: whether the trials excluded or recorded other drug use is not described.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. Five of the six trials treated inpatients or medical-centre patients, where continued use is limited, so improvement within each arm is confounded with abstinence and the passage of time.

comparison.controls: Another antipsychotic in five trials (haloperidol, risperidone, aripiprazole, quetiapine or olanzapine) and placebo in one (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (randomized trials). Baseline balance is not reported, except that in one trial (Verachai 2014) symptom scores were higher at baseline in the haloperidol arm (Results › Clinical Benefits › Haloperidol, Quetiapine).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of psychosis, duration and amount of use, and earlier psychotic episodes are not reported for any trial; earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder was an exclusion criterion in all of them.

outcomes.instruments: PANSS (Verachai, Wang, Sulaiman), SAPS and SANS (Farnia), SAPS (Samiei), BPRS and CGI-S (Leelahanaj), CGI-S (Wang); side effects by trial-specific measures (Simpson–Angus Scale, Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale, AIMS, adverse-event counts); retention, completion or dropout (Table 2; Table 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard psychosis rating scales; the review reports no baseline severity for any trial.
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy: reduction of psychotic symptoms on the trial's scale. Risks: side effects such as akathisia, agitation, hypotension and sedation, and serious adverse events such as neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Secondary: retention, completion and dropout (Methods › Types of Outcome Measures). Effect size: the standardized mean difference between the two groups where means and SDs were available, otherwise percentages (Methods › Measures of Treatment Effect). Which groups, time points and direction each SMD in Table 3 expresses is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three outcome domains (efficacy, side effects, retention) are summarized trial by trial; Table 3 gives 13 per-trial SMDs on different scales and time points without correction (editors' count).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Two authors separately searched, screened abstracts, extracted data and scored trial quality, and a third author settled disagreements (Methods › Data Extraction, Quality Assessment, and Assessment of Risk of Bias; Author contributions).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate; heterogeneity was not assessed because the data were judged not combinable (Methods › Assessment of Heterogeneity; Data Synthesis and Analysis). Per-trial SMDs computed by the authors (Table 3), as printed: Verachai 2014 (quetiapine vs haloperidol) 0.7602 (95% CI 0.2662 to 1.2542) on PANSS and 0.2914 (0.1514 to 0.7341) on cure rate; Wang 2016 (aripiprazole vs risperidone) 0.6601 (0.039 to 1.2812) on PANSS at days 1 to 7 and 0.0617 (−0.5433 to 0.6667) at days 10 to 16, 0.6202 (0.0009 to 1.2394) and 0 (−0.6049 to 0.6049) on CGI-S; Farnia 2014 (aripiprazole vs risperidone) −1 (−1.6199 to 0.3801) on SAPS and −0.7746 (−1.3806 to 0.1686) on SANS; Samiei 2016 (haloperidol vs risperidone) 0.8895 (0.0134 to 1.7655) overall, 0.2141 (−0.3786 to 0.8067) for hallucinations, 0.5116 (−0.0889 to 1.1122) for delusions and 0.6023 (−0.0019 to 1.2065) for bizarre behaviour; Leelahanaj 2005 (olanzapine vs haloperidol) 0.912 (0.3712 to 1.4528) on end-point CGI-S and BPRS. Placebo-controlled trial (Sulaiman 2013): symptoms fell more on aripiprazole than on placebo (p < 0.005 in the text, p < 0.05 in Table 3); no SMD calculable. Editors' check: four of the intervals are symmetric about their estimates only if minus signs were lost (reporting issue 1).
analysis.covariates: None at review level; the text notes that one trial's end-point comparison was adjusted for demographic data (Verachai 2014).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the methods state that the review follows PRISMA.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-trial risk-of-bias judgments are given only in a supplement (not read); the article gives a summary. The SMDs come without the comparison or direction they express, and several have intervals that exclude zero where the review's own text, or the same table cell, reports no significant difference between the drugs (Verachai at the end point; Leelahanaj, p = 0.37).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The trials had 37 to 80 participants (editors' sums from Table 2).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six small randomized trials (37 to 80 participants, 25 days to 8 weeks). In every trial symptoms fell within both arms; differences between drugs varied in direction with the measure and time point, and the review's effect sizes cannot show which were significant; in the one placebo-controlled trial (37 participants) symptoms fell more on aripiprazole, which caused more akathisia and agitation. No trial followed participants after it ended.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state that antipsychotics seem efficacious on positive and negative symptoms and that the five drugs controlled psychosis "with no adverse event" (Abstract › Results); the discussion calls them effective and safe (Discussion › Summary of Main Findings). Gaps: (1) efficacy is inferred from improvement within each arm of head-to-head trials, which cannot separate a drug effect from recovery with abstinence and time, a possibility the authors raise themselves when they say the psychosis may be self-limited (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph); (2) 'no adverse event' contrasts with the akathisia, agitation and dystonia reported on aripiprazole, the discontinuation of about one-third of participants because of extrapyramidal symptoms in the olanzapine–haloperidol trial (where 65.5% completed haloperidol), and the higher dropout on aripiprazole in the placebo-controlled trial; (3) the abstract says no drug was clinically superior, while the discussion says aripiprazole reduced psychosis better than risperidone in two trials, which the Results do not show (the two trials' results run in both directions), and that haloperidol seemed superior to risperidone, which rests on item-level differences in one trial in weeks 1 to 3 whose Table 3 intervals all include zero; (4) the Conclusions say the trials lacked placebo-controlled arms, although one included trial was placebo-controlled; (5) every trial is graded low (GRADE 'R+', further research very likely to change the estimate) in Table 2, which the abstract does not mention.

timeline.event: Cochrane review of treatment for amphetamine psychosis (Shoptaw, Kao and Ling), cited by this review as finding olanzapine and haloperidol both efficacious with different side-effect profiles (Discussion › Summary of Main Findings; reference 54).
Narrative review of methamphetamine psychosis describing the Cochrane review's single trial and a later haloperidol–quetiapine trial
This review: six randomized trials, 314 participants, searches to November 2018.

Network meta-analysis that searched this review's reference list: six head-to-head trials, five of them shared with this review; it excluded the placebo-controlled aripiprazole trial (participants' symptoms had subsided) and added a 2020 paliperidone–risperidone trial

Systematic review that includes all six of this review's trials among eight randomized trials in amphetamine-induced psychosis and reads one aripiprazole–risperidone trial (Farnia 2014) differently from this review
24-month randomized trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against treatment as usual, which cites this review for broadly comparable short-term efficacy of the antipsychotics

replication.where_it_stands: Superseded as an inventory by the 2021 network meta-analysis (searches to June 2020) and the 2026 systematic review (to March 2026), which contain its trials, so it adds no independent evidence; what it adds is the inclusion and a summary of the placebo-controlled aripiprazole trial. Its per-trial effect sizes, and its account of one aripiprazole–risperidone trial, conflict with its own text and with the later reviews, and should not be cited without the trial reports.

funding.funder: Not reported (the article has no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that the research was conducted without commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Emory University School of Medicine (Atlanta), the Department of Psychiatry at NYU Langone Health (New York) and the Department of Health, Miami Regional University (Miami Springs). One of the two named peer reviewers, Vahid Farnia (Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences, Iran), has the family name and initial of the first author of an included trial (Farnia et al., 2014, reference 50); the article does not say whether they are the same person. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A double-blind randomized trial in people admitted with acute methamphetamine psychosis comparing an antipsychotic with placebo on top of supervised abstinence and standard care, with time to remission as the primary outcome, side effects measured the same way in both arms, and follow-up after the drug is stopped.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (amphetamine psychosis, any age, inpatients or outpatients), intervention (antipsychotics), comparator (another antipsychotic or placebo) and outcomes (efficacy, side effects, retention) are stated (Methods).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Only randomized trials were included; the choice is stated (focusing on controlled clinical trials) but not explained.

Eight databases plus ClinicalTrials.gov and grey literature, no language restriction, keywords listed, and a search within 24 months of publication. Not met for 'yes': the keywords were amphetamine terms only (no methamphetamine term, no drug names), no full strategy, no reference-list searching or expert consultation reported, and a 2018 randomized trial cited in the discussion was neither captured nor explained.
Two authors separately searched, screened abstracts and retained articles; a third settled disagreements (Methods › Data Extraction, Quality Assessment, and Assessment of Risk of Bias).
Two authors separately extracted and analysed the data (Author contributions).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Eight full texts were assessed and the two excluded are named with their reasons (Results › Description of Studies; references 46 and 47).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives arm sizes, setting, country, age range, design, duration, doses, rating scales and diagnostic criteria; sex, baseline severity and substance-use characteristics are not given per trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (selection, performance, detection, attrition and reporting bias) and Jadad scores; the text gives only a summary (no trial at high risk of selection bias, two at high risk of performance and detection bias, about 85% of trials at low risk overall), with per-trial judgments in an unread supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: The methods say funding disclosures were collected, but none are reported.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Each trial is graded low in Table 2, but the conclusions (efficacious, effective and safe) take no account of the trials' risk of bias, of the two trials without double blinding, or of the absence of a placebo arm in five trials.

Heterogeneity is invoked (the GRADE level was given per trial because of elevated heterogeneity; data not combinable) but its sources are not investigated or discussed in relation to the conflicting trial results.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no conflicts of interest; the article has no funding statement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (2: no protocol; 13: risk of bias not taken into account in the conclusions) and two are only partly met (4 and 9), which gives critically low confidence. The review may be cited for its inventory of six trials to November 2018, including the placebo-controlled aripiprazole trial, and for the trial-level side-effect and retention figures it reports, with the caveats in the reporting issues. Its efficacy conclusions and its per-trial SMDs should not be cited: the SMDs do not say what they compare, several intervals appear to have lost minus signs, and the efficacy claim rests on improvement within each arm.

key_findings.finding: Searches of eight databases plus ClinicalTrials.gov and grey literature from inception to November 2018 (keywords: amphetamine, amphetamine psychosis, amphetamine-induced psychosis and amphetamine psychosis-controlled trials) gave 643 titles; 39 documents were screened, 8 full articles assessed and 6 randomized trials included. The two excluded full texts were a randomized trial that did not concern amphetamine psychosis and a non-randomized open-label aripiprazole study.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Materials and Methods › Search Strategy; Results › Description of Studies

key_findings.finding: Six randomized trials, 314 participants: quetiapine 36 vs haloperidol 44 (Verachai 2014, Thailand, inpatients, 4 weeks, double-blind); aripiprazole 21 vs risperidone 21 (Wang 2016, China, inpatients, 25 days, not double-blind); aripiprazole 27 vs risperidone 26 (Farnia 2014, Iran, inpatients, 6 weeks, double-blind, amphetamine-induced psychosis); aripiprazole 19 vs placebo 18 (Sulaiman 2013, Malaysia, medical centre, 8 weeks, double-blind, placebo-controlled); haloperidol 22 vs risperidone 22 (Samiei 2016, Iran, inpatients, 1 month, not double-blind); olanzapine 29 vs haloperidol 29 (Leelahanaj 2005, Thailand, outpatients, 4 weeks, double-blind, amphetamine psychosis). Five trials are head-to-head; one is placebo-controlled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' sums from Table 2 match the 314 of the abstract. The olanzapine–haloperidol trial is listed with 29 and 29 (58); the 2021 network meta-analysis lists 29 and 27 (study card sc_srisurapanont_2021).

key_findings.finding: Every trial was given the GRADE level 'R+' (further research very likely to change the estimate; low), mainly for small samples and design limitations; four trials scored 4 and two scored 3 on the Jadad scale. Risk of bias (summary only): no trial at high risk of selection bias, two at high risk of performance and detection bias, none at risk of attrition or reporting bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of Bias in Included Studies, 1st paragraph; Results › Synthesis of Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and its notes

key_findings.finding: Nothing was pooled: the data were judged not combinable, heterogeneity was not assessed and a meta-analysis was not possible; results are given trial by trial with per-trial SMDs (Table 3).
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Assessment of Heterogeneity; Data Synthesis and Analysis

key_findings.finding: Head-to-head trials, as the text reports them: symptoms fell from baseline in both arms of four of the five trials (no within-arm change is reported for Verachai 2014). Farnia 2014: risperidone better on positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, bizarre behaviour, thought disorder) and aripiprazole better on negative symptoms; Wang 2016: aripiprazole better on PANSS in days 1 to 7, risperidone slightly better in days 10 to 16; Verachai 2014: no significant difference on PANSS at the end point after adjustment, quetiapine ahead in a generalized-estimating-equation analysis, and time to cure slightly favouring haloperidol; Samiei 2016: haloperidol ahead on hallucinations, delusions and bizarre behaviour in weeks 1 to 3 (Table 3 intervals include zero); Leelahanaj 2005: both improved (p < 0.001), small non-significant difference on CGI-S favouring olanzapine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical Benefits (subsections Aripiprazole, Risperidone; Haloperidol, Quetiapine; Haloperidol, Risperidone; Haloperidol, Olanzapine), 1st paragraph each; Table 3
key_findings.note: For Farnia 2014, Table 3's labels say the opposite of the text (aripiprazole better on SAPS, risperidone better on SANS); see reporting issue 2. For Verachai 2014, Table 3 labels the cure-rate SMD as slightly favouring quetiapine (reporting issue 13). The subsections cite Table 2 for results that are in Table 3.

key_findings.finding: Placebo-controlled trial (Sulaiman 2013; aripiprazole 19, placebo 18; 8 weeks): Table 3 says psychotic symptoms fell more on aripiprazole than on placebo (p < 0.05); the text gives p < 0.005 for aripiprazole's reduction of PANSS severity without naming the comparison, and mean CGI-S 2 on aripiprazole and 2.1 on placebo without a time point. Aripiprazole caused more akathisia and agitation and less insomnia, and dropout was higher on aripiprazole on days 28 and 58 (text).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical Benefits › Aripiprazole, Placebo, 1st paragraph; Results › Side Effects and Serious Adverse Events › Aripiprazole, Placebo; Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout › Aripiprazole, Risperidone (last sentence); Table 3, Sulaiman row
key_findings.note: A mean CGI-S of about 2 in both arms, at a time point the review does not state, indicates little illness at that point; the review does not give the participants' symptom level at entry.

key_findings.finding: Side effects and retention reported per trial: no neuroleptic malignant syndrome or other life-threatening event in any trial. Wang 2016: agitation 52.4% vs 19.0%, akathisia 61.9% vs 28.6%, dystonia 86% vs 29% and discontinuation 33% vs 0% on aripiprazole vs risperidone, retention 19.9 vs 24 days; extrapyramidal scores rose in both arms without a significant difference. Leelahanaj 2005: completers 93.1% on olanzapine vs 65.5% on haloperidol, haloperidol causing more extrapyramidal symptoms, hypertonia, dyskinesia and hypersalivation and olanzapine more somnolence (15.4% vs 7.4%), headache, weight gain and rash. Verachai 2014: completers 31 of 36 on quetiapine vs 37 of 44 on haloperidol. Farnia 2014: no extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation or akathisia. Samiei 2016: no adverse-event or retention data.
key_findings.locator: Results › Side Effects and Serious Adverse Events (all subsections); Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout (all subsections); Table 3
key_findings.note: Several percentages do not fit the arm sizes they are attributed to (reporting issues 4 and 5).

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: few and small trials; only one placebo-controlled trial; the longest trial lasted 8 weeks and none followed participants after the trial, so long-term benefit and prevention of further episodes are unknown; the side effects reported are those of the drugs in primary psychoses and may not be specific to amphetamine psychosis.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations; Discussion › Balancing Risk and Efficacy of Atypical/Typical Antipsychotics; Consideration of the Use of Long-Acting Antipsychotics

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that antipsychotics are efficacious and clinically relevant for amphetamine psychosis while noting that the psychosis may be self-limited and may respond to any antipsychotic; they judge treatment with antipsychotics clinically and ethically appropriate and are unsure whether more placebo-controlled trials are needed, given ethical and legal difficulties.

reporting_issues.issue: Four confidence intervals in Table 3 are symmetric about their estimates only if minus signs were lost: Verachai's 0.2914 is printed with 0.1514 to 0.7341 (symmetric: −0.1514 to 0.7341), and Farnia's −1 and −0.7746 with upper limits 0.3801 and 0.1686 (symmetric: −0.3801 and −0.1686). Every other interval in the table is symmetric as printed (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (Verachai and Farnia rows)
reporting_issues.consequence: As printed, the Verachai interval excludes zero when it should not, and the Farnia intervals include zero when they should not; the table cannot be used without correction.

reporting_issues.issue: For Farnia 2014 the Results text says risperidone was better on positive symptoms and aripiprazole on negative symptoms, Table 3 labels the SMDs the other way round (aripiprazole better on SAPS, risperidone better on SANS), and the discussion says aripiprazole reduced psychosis better than risperidone in two trials.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Clinical Benefits › Aripiprazole, Risperidone; Table 3; Discussion › Summary of Main Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of this trial's between-drug result cannot be taken from this review; the 2026 systematic review reads it as favouring aripiprazole on positive symptoms (study card sc_hall_2026), and the trial report has not been read.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 does not say which groups, time points or direction each SMD compares, and some SMDs have intervals that exclude zero beside a cell that reports no significant between-drug difference or a change within both arms: Leelahanaj 0.912 (0.3712 to 1.4528) in the same cell as p = 0.37; Samiei 0.8895 (0.0134 to 1.7655) labelled as both drugs reducing psychosis. Verachai's 0.7602 (0.2662 to 1.2542), labelled as quetiapine better, matches the text's generalized-estimating-equation result but not its adjusted end-point comparison (no significant difference).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3; Results › Clinical Benefits
reporting_issues.consequence: The SMDs may express change within arms or something else; they cannot be read as between-drug effect sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Verachai row, the side-effect percentages fit the arm sizes only with the drug labels exchanged: hypotension 2.3% (1 of 44) is attributed to quetiapine (36 participants) and 5.6% (2 of 36) to haloperidol (44); sedation 9.1% (4 of 44) to quetiapine and 8.3% (3 of 36) to haloperidol (editors' arithmetic). The Results text says quetiapine caused more sedation, the discussion that it caused less.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (Verachai row); Results › Side Effects and Serious Adverse Events › Haloperidol, Quetiapine; Discussion › Summary of Main Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: Which of the two drugs caused more hypotension and sedation cannot be read from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Leelahanaj row, side-effect percentages imply denominators of 26 on olanzapine (15.4% = 4 of 26, 3.8% = 1 of 26, 7.7% = 2 of 26) and 27 on haloperidol (7.4% = 2 of 27), while the completer percentages fit 29 and 29 (93.1% = 27 of 29, 65.5% = 19 of 29) (editors' arithmetic). The retention text also calls this trial a comparison of olanzapine with risperidone; it compared olanzapine with haloperidol.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (Leelahanaj row); Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout › Haloperidol, Olanzapine
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial's arm sizes differ between reviews (29 and 29 here and in the 2026 review; 29 and 27 in the network meta-analysis); the side-effect denominators (26 and 27) match neither the randomized arms nor the completers (27 and 19), so what the percentages are shares of cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The review gives the number of participants per trial as a mean of 26.16 (SD 7.61); these are the mean and SD of the 12 arm sizes, and the mean per trial is 52.3 (editors' calculation from Table 2). The mean age of 32 with an SD of 20.63 is not plausible for trials of people aged 15 or 18 and over.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Synthesis of Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's descriptive statistics are unreliable; the trial sizes should be taken from Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: For the placebo-controlled trial the text gives p < 0.005 and Table 3 p < 0.05; Table 3's 'dropout rate' (aripiprazole 83% after 27 days and 82% after 58 days, placebo 66% and 44%) cannot be a cumulative dropout, which could not fall between day 27 and day 58 as both arms' figures do; read as retention, it contradicts the text's higher dropout on aripiprazole; and the text gives the days as 28 and 58. The side-effect entries for the same trial pair 'akathisia' with AIMS scores (a dyskinesia scale), 'agitation' with BARS scores (glossed as a Brief Agitation Rating Scale, while the text uses the Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale) and 'insomnia' with Simpson–Angus scores, and repeat the values 10.6 and 5.6.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (Sulaiman row) and its footnote; Results › Clinical Benefits › Aripiprazole, Placebo; Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout
reporting_issues.consequence: Retention and side effects in the only placebo-controlled trial cannot be read from this review; the 2026 review gives the trial's between-group p as 0.032 (study card sc_hall_2026).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the drugs worked with no adverse event and that no drug was clinically superior; the Results report akathisia, agitation and dystonia on aripiprazole and, in the olanzapine–haloperidol trial, discontinuation of about one-third of participants because of extrapyramidal symptoms, and the discussion says aripiprazole was better than risperidone in two trials and haloperidol seemed superior to risperidone. The Conclusions say the trials lacked placebo-controlled arms, although one included trial had one.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout › Haloperidol, Olanzapine; Discussion › Summary of Main Findings; Discussion › Conclusions, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract and conclusions do not match the results; claims should cite the trial-level results, not the review's summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The risk-of-bias summary says about 85% of the trials were at low risk of bias overall (5 of 6 would be 83%), while the same paragraph puts two of the six trials at high risk of performance and detection bias, which would leave at most four of six (67%) at low risk in every domain.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Risk of Bias in Included Studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the per-trial judgments are only in the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: A randomized trial of olanzapine against haloperidol in mental disorders induced by amphetamine-type stimulants, published in 2018 within the search period (Xue et al., reference 63), is cited in the discussion but neither included nor listed among the excluded studies; the search used only amphetamine keywords.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion › Psycho-Pharmacological Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Materials and Methods › Search Strategy; reference 63
reporting_issues.consequence: The inventory may be incomplete; the 2021 network meta-analysis excluded the same trial because the diagnosis was unclear (study card sc_srisurapanont_2021).

reporting_issues.issue: The summary of main findings attributes to one trial both longer retention on aripiprazole and more akathisia and agitation on aripiprazole; the Results give the longer retention on aripiprazole in one trial (Farnia) and the akathisia, agitation and shorter retention on aripiprazole in another (Wang).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion › Summary of Main Findings; Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout › Aripiprazole, Risperidone
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the trial-level results should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The search yield is given as 643 titles, but the per-source counts printed in the same sentence (126, 70, 195, 164, 39, 2, 116, 77 and 49) add up to 838 (editors' sum); no removal of duplicates is described, while 643 minus the 604 removed on titles and abstracts gives the 39 documents screened.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Description of Studies
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the flow from records found to documents screened cannot be reconstructed from the text (the PRISMA diagram is an image).

reporting_issues.issue: For Verachai 2014, Table 3 labels the cure-rate SMD (0.2914) as quetiapine slightly superior to haloperidol, while the text says time to cure slightly favoured haloperidol; the review does not say whether these are the same measure.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (Verachai row); Results › Clinical Benefits › Haloperidol, Quetiapine
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of this trial's secondary result cannot be taken from this review.

disagreements.first_pass: Head-to-head trials, as the text reports them: symptoms fell from baseline in both arms of every trial. … Verachai 2014: no significant difference on PANSS at the end point after adjustment, quetiapine ahead in a generalized-estimating-equation analysis;
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: corrected: 'symptoms fell from baseline in both arms of every trial' is not stated for Verachai 2014, for which the review gives only the adjusted end-point comparison (no significant difference), the GEE result (quetiapine ahead) and time to cure (a slight difference favouring haloperidol, omitted from the finding); within-arm reductions are stated for the other four head-to-head trials. Missed: Table 3's cure-rate label for Verachai favours quetiapine; the Clinical Benefits subsections cite Table 2 for results that are in Table 3.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Results › Clinical Benefits (subsections Aripiprazole, Risperidone; Haloperidol, Quetiapine; Haloperidol, Risperidone; Haloperidol, Olanzapine): within-arm reductions are reported for Farnia, Wang 2016, Samiei and Leelahanaj, not for Verachai, whose paragraph ends with time to cure slightly favouring haloperidol. Finding reworded to four of the five trials, time to cure added; the note points to the new reporting issue 13 and records the Table 2 cross-reference slip.

disagreements.first_pass: psychotic symptoms on the PANSS fell more on aripiprazole than on placebo (p < 0.005 in the text; p < 0.05 in Table 3); mean CGI-S at the end 2 on aripiprazole and 2.1 on placebo. … A CGI-S of about 2 at the end of the trial in both arms indicates little residual illness; the review does not give the participants' symptom level at entry.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: corrected: the review gives mean CGI-S 2 on aripiprazole and 2.1 on placebo without a time point ('at the end' is not in the text); the comparison with placebo is from Table 3, and the text's p < 0.005 for aripiprazole reducing PANSS severity does not name the comparison; the note's 'at the end of the trial' rests on the unstated time point.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Results › Clinical Benefits › Aripiprazole, Placebo (p < 0.005 for the reduction on aripiprazole; CGI-S 2 and 2.1, no time point) and Table 3, Sulaiman row (decreased more than placebo, p < 0.05). Finding and note reworded; side effects and dropout unchanged (confirmed).

disagreements.first_pass: and several SMDs have intervals that exclude zero where the review's own text or the same cell reports no significant between-drug difference: Verachai 0.7602 (0.2662 to 1.2542) beside a text reporting no significant end-point difference; Leelahanaj 0.912 (0.3712 to 1.4528) in the same cell as p = 0.37; Samiei 0.8895 (0.0134 to 1.7655) labelled as both drugs reducing psychosis.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: corrected: the core issue stands, but the Verachai example is weaker than written: the text reports no significant end-point difference after adjustment and also a GEE analysis in which quetiapine reduced symptoms more, and Table 3's label for 0.7602 matches the GEE result; the Leelahanaj and Samiei examples stand.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 3 (Verachai cell: 'quetiapine reduced PANSS score better than haloperidol') and Results › Clinical Benefits › Haloperidol, Quetiapine. Verachai moved from the list of contradictions to a qualified example; consequence unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: the side effects may be counted among people who stayed in the trial.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: confirmed, with a note: the consequence's suggestion that side effects were counted among those who stayed does not fit the haloperidol arm (denominator 27, but 19 completers).
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed from Table 3: 15.4%, 3.8% and 7.7% fit 26 on olanzapine, 7.4% fits 27 on haloperidol, and the completer percentages (93.1%, 65.5%) give 27 and 19 of 29. Neither arm fits the suggestion, so the consequence now says only what the numbers show.

disagreements.first_pass: Table 3's 'dropout rate' (aripiprazole 83% after 27 days and 82% after 58 days, placebo 66% and 44%) cannot be dropout if most participants completed, reads as retention but then contradicts the text's higher dropout on aripiprazole, and the text gives the days as 28 and 58.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: confirmed, with a firmer reason than the card's conditional: the 'dropout rate' falls from day 27 to day 58 in both arms (83% to 82%, 66% to 44%), which a cumulative dropout cannot do.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 3 (Sulaiman row) and Results › Treatment Retention, Completion, and Dropout. The reason is arithmetic, so it replaces the conditional; the rest of the issue is unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: The risk-of-bias summary says about 85% of the trials were at low risk of bias, which is not a possible share of six trials (5 of 6 is 83%), alongside two trials at high risk of performance and detection bias.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: corrected: the text says 'about 85%', which 5 of 6 (83%) satisfies, so the share is not impossible by itself; the tension is with the two trials at high risk of performance and detection bias, which would leave at most 4 of 6 (67%) at low risk in every domain.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Results › Risk of Bias in Included Studies, 1st paragraph. Issue reworded; consequence (minor) unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: differences between drugs varied with the measure and time point and were mostly not significant in the trials' own analyses; … (3) the abstract says no drug was clinically superior, while the discussion says aripiprazole reduced psychosis better than risperidone in two trials and that haloperidol seemed superior to risperidone, neither of which the Results show;
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: agree (substantial), with two wording corrections: the Results text does state that haloperidol was superior to risperidone on hallucination, delusion and bizarre behaviour in weeks 1 to 3 (it is Table 3's intervals, all including zero, that do not support it); and the review reports significant item-level differences in Farnia 2014 (both directions) and superiority in Wang 2016 and Samiei 2016, non-significance only for Verachai at the end point and Leelahanaj, so 'mostly not significant' should read that differences varied in direction and the effect sizes cannot show which were significant.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Results › Clinical Benefits (each subsection) and Table 3. Both passages reworded as the reader proposes; gap rating (substantial) unchanged.
